messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Hotel Manager
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar People: Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar, Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Vignette:
Marisol Alvarez is a 37-year-old hotel manager who came to treatment after many months of trying to keep herself moving fast enough that she would not have to sit still with what happened. She is in a long-term relationship, and from the outside she appears highly competent: polished at work, endlessly available, the person who stays late when a guest crisis unfolds or when staffing falls apart. When she first began describing the assault, though, she kept stopping mid-sentence, pressing her lips together, and saying that she knew what happened but could not find the words to say it straight. Even to herself, the night came back in fragments rather than as a story she could follow from beginning to end.

The assault occurred after a hotel industry social event, the kind of networking gathering she had attended many times as part of her job. She had been with people she knew professionally, including a man who was part of that wider circle. In recounting the evening, Marisol could identify pieces with painful clarity—the end of the event, the sense of being cornered, the shock of her own body freezing and reacting while her mind seemed to fall behind—but when she tried to join those pieces together she became overwhelmed and lost track of what came first and what followed. She would lower her eyes and say that talking about it made her feel filthy and exposed. The strongest feeling attached to the memory was shame: shame not only about what was done to her, but shame that she could not narrate it cleanly, as if her inability to tell it properly meant something about her.

In the weeks afterward, Marisol did not speak about the assault in any full way. She had come to believe there was something wrong with her as a person, that this had happened because of the sort of woman she was. She described a harsh, repetitive line of thinking in which the event seemed to confirm that she was somehow defective. What frightened her as much as the memory itself was her body. A cologne in an elevator, a man at the hotel bar with a similar build or haircut, the sound of laughter from a group leaving a conference room—her heart would race, her stomach would drop, and her muscles would tense before she had even fully registered why. She was certain these reactions meant her body had become an enemy to her, acting as if danger were still present even when she was standing behind the front desk at midday with staff all around her. She did not experience those reactions as understandable reminders; she experienced them as further evidence that something inside her was damaged.

At work, the hotel became both refuge and trap. Because she manages a busy property, there were always emails to answer, staffing schedules to revise, guest complaints to smooth over, vendors to call. Marisol began arriving early and staying late, volunteering to cover problems that could have waited until morning. She told herself she was being responsible, but she also knew that if she went home too early and had an empty evening, her mind would circle back to the assault. Work gave her noise, decisions, fluorescent light, and other people’s needs. It let her postpone being alone with her thoughts. Her boyfriend noticed she was disappearing into the job, canceling dinners and coming home exhausted and unreachable. She could not explain it clearly to him any more than she could to herself; she only knew that stillness felt dangerous.

She also became acutely vigilant around certain guests and industry contacts. If someone who resembled the assailant came through the lobby, or if she learned that people connected to that night might attend an event at the hotel, she rearranged her duties so another manager would handle the floor. She avoided social functions where she might encounter anyone involved or anyone who looked similar enough to set off that immediate surge in her body. These choices narrowed her world over time. Colleagues began to notice that she was oddly selective about which events she attended. Her boyfriend experienced her as distant and preoccupied, especially on nights when she sat awake, turning over fantasies of revenge. In those hours she would mentally rehearse how she might get even with the man who assaulted her, imagining confrontation, exposure, or some form of payback that might make the balance feel less unbearable. The thoughts did not settle her, but she returned to them repeatedly.

By the time Marisol sought help, she was exhausted by the effort of holding herself together. What finally pushed her toward treatment was a recent moment at the hotel when she saw a guest from across the lobby who looked enough like the man from that night that her body reacted instantly; afterward she locked herself in her office, shaking and unable to explain to a colleague why she suddenly could not continue a routine shift. She came in saying she needed help putting words to something that still felt unspeakable. Most of all, she was afraid that the assault had revealed who she truly was—that defective, shameful self she believed she had been trying to hide—and at the same time she was hoping, cautiously, that there might be a way to remember what happened without feeling that her body and her whole character had turned against her.
